name: Trooper
lede: Trooper is a dark navy blue from the Maerz and Paul color dictionary, one of a cluster of near-identical navies the 1930 book recorded under different names.

sections.title: One navy among several
sections.body:
Maerz and Paul record Trooper at #192D45, first dated 1919, on plate 40 L9 of their 1930 dictionary [1]. The same plate carries three other names within a few units of this value: Corsair (1920), Ispahan (1925) and Labrador, the oldest of the group at 1892 [1]. A fourth, Nippon (1921), sits close by as well [1]; the books do not explain why the dictionary split one dark navy into so many names, so that choice is undocumented here [1].

Its nearest named neighbor in our library is [[bagdad]], a touch lighter and less blue [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Our archive finds this hue, as photographed, in 195 of 23,781 paintings (0.82 percent), more common than 60 percent of the named colors we track [2]. It peaks in the 1900s, in 22 of 1,674 paintings, at 2.5 times the expected rate for paintings from that century [2]. Inside a painting it most often turns up as a hidden color, in the darkest part of the canvas, in 53 percent of its 110 occurrences [2].

The earliest matching painting in our archive is dated 1099, 831 years before Maerz and Paul recorded the name in 1930, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [2]. No single painter stands out here by a wide margin, so no devoted-painter figure is given [2]. It sits among the darkest named colors in our library, comparably dark to [[umbra-grey]] and to the RAL grey [[traffic-grey-b]], though neither is a close hue match [2].

openers: Trooper is one of five near-identical dark navies that Maerz and Paul recorded on a single 1930 plate.
